chunks: Muhammad ibn Aḥmad ibn Yaḥyā, from Muḥammad ibn ʿĪsā, from al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī ibn Faḍḍāl, who said:
I read in the book of Abū al-Asad to Abū al-Ḥasan al-Thānī (peace be upon him), and I read it by his own hand:
He asked him: What is the interpretation of His Exalted Saying, 'And do not consume one another's wealth unjustly, nor send it [as a bribe] to the rulers'?
He said, so he wrote to him in his own hand: 'The rulers are the judges.'

He said, then he wrote below it: 'It is that a man knows that he is the oppressor, so the judge rules in his favor; he is not excused in taking that which the judge ruled for him, if he had known that he was the oppressor.'

key_terms.الْحُكَّامُ: The rulers (specifically judges in this context)

ai.seo_question: What is the meaning of 'rulers' in the verse about consuming wealth unjustly?
ai.summary: This narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* elucidates the term 'al-ḥukkām' in Quran 2:188 as referring specifically to judges, highlighting the mechanism of unjust wealth consumption through legal manipulation. It establishes that a litigant who knows they are in the wrong (ẓālim) but secures a favorable ruling is not excused, as the judgment serves as the vehicle for their unjust appropriation. This underscores the Shia jurisprudential emphasis on the substantive justice of the transaction rather than merely its procedural validity.
